# Commands

spec

`docc init` creates `docc.json`, `docs/schemas/page.json` and `docs/src/index.json` (kind page) if they do not exist and builds `docs/out`, so the first check is green. The configuration it writes has `maxWarnings` 0, so a warning such as a stale link (DOC209) fails `docc check`, and it adds the single-file builds (`docs/out.md`, `docs/out.html`, `docs/out-full*`) to `.gitignore`. In a git repository without a pre-commit hook it also writes `.git/hooks/pre-commit`, which runs `docc check`, so a commit with invalid documentation is refused; an existing hook is never touched.

`docc validate` checks the sources and prints the diagnostics. It changes no files.

`docc build` first gives a code to every block without one (as `docc codes`), then writes the Markdown into `docs/out` and removes the files it generated earlier that no source produces any more (pages with the GENERATED mark, copies of images, file manager junk). When the folder holds any other file it refuses with exit code 2, writes and deletes nothing and lists those files. When the sources have errors of the groups 1xx or 2xx it writes nothing and exits with code 1, except a link whose version hash is missing or old (DOC209) and a block without a code (DOC216): then it writes the pages and exits with code 1, so a draft stays readable while an agent checks the hashes. With the flag full it writes the audit build into `docs/out-full` and leaves `docs/out` alone.

The flags single and html add one file next to the folder, each can be combined with full: `docc build --single` writes all pages into one Markdown file (`docs/out.md`) and `docc build --html` into one self-contained HTML application (`docs/out.html`) to read and comment on: a timeline of the saved versions with the edits drawn in the text, and comments ([Rendering](rendering.md)). The HTML file also holds the object of `docc workspace` in `<script id="docc-workspace" type="application/json">`, hidden documents included, for the reader of Docspace embedded in docc; until that reader is embedded (`scripts/update-reader.sh`) the file is the application described here, with the object beside its data. A build that changes only the time of the object leaves the file as it is. The folder of pages is built as before. Once made, such a file is rebuilt by every later `docc build`, with or without the flag, so a stale file is never sent, if docc wrote it; a file of another origin is left alone with a message on stderr, and only the flag replaces it. `--since <revision>` names the version a reader last saw (a tag, branch or commit): the HTML file shows the edits since it and keeps no history before it; a bad revision stops only the HTML file: the diagnostics are still printed and the exit code is 2. `--page <path>` writes one page alone: its path relative to the source folder as `docc compile` gives it (with or without `.json`) or its id; the output folder gets only that page and the pictures it shows (no other page, no `_tree.md`, until a build without the flag), and the one-file builds hold only that page; an unknown page, or a hidden one without full, is an error with exit code 2. `--rev <revision>` builds the tree of a Git revision without a checkout, as `docc compile --rev` reads it (a bare mirror with `--config` too): it needs `--html`, refuses `--single` and writes only the HTML file, into the current folder, with the history up to that revision; the output folder and `docc.lock` are not written. The readers' comments stand under their blocks in the pages and the HTML file, and `--no-comments` leaves them out of everything the build writes. `--codes` is for print: in the Markdown (the pages and `docs/out.md`) the code of every block stands in bold before its text (`**PAY-14** Text`), or as a line of its own before a list, table, quote, code block or heading, so a printed page names the blocks other documents cite; the anchor of a linked block stands before it. The HTML file is not changed: it shows a block's code on hover. `docc check` accepts `docs/out` built with or without the flag, and a later build without it writes the pages without codes. These files are for reading, are not committed and are not checked by `docc check`. With full they are `docs/out-full.md` and `docs/out-full.html`.

`docc watch` is for reading the documents and the work on them while an agent writes them. It builds as `docc build` does (the Markdown folder, and the one-file builds docc wrote before; `--full` and `--no-comments` work as in build) and then looks every quarter of a second at the sources, the schemas, `docc.json`, the folders of `trace.scan` and the run file of the `workspace` section ([Configuration](config.md)); when they have been still for a second (at most three seconds after the first save) it builds again. A change of the run file alone builds nothing: it only sends the workspace again. At `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` it serves the reader (`GET /`), the object of `docc workspace` (`GET /workspace.json`) and Server-Sent Events (`GET /events`): `event: workspace` with the time of the object, at once and after every change, and the reader fetches the object again without a reload. A build that stops at errors keeps the last pages and says why in the terminal. The port comes from the path of the project, so it is the same every time and other projects get other ports; a busy port is an error, and there is no flag to change it. The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only, answers GET for the page, the object, the events and `GET /diff?base=<rev>&head=<rev>` and nothing else, and refuses a request whose Host or Origin is not its own address, so a page of another site that points its name at 127.0.0.1 cannot read the documents. It writes exactly one thing: `POST /answer` with `{"doc": <id>, "answer": <text>}` (a JSON body of at most 16 KiB, from 127.0.0.1 only) sets the field «Ответ» of a document whose kind plays the questions role, keeping the block code of the field and every other byte of the file; the save starts the build like any edit. With the answer it writes the value fields `answeredBy` (`git config user.name`, left out when empty) and `answeredAt` (UTC, RFC 3339). When nothing is staged (`git diff --cached --quiet`) it commits exactly that file with the message `Ответ человека: <title>` and the trailer `Crew-Actor: human`; without git, or when the commit fails, the answer stays written. Then, when `workspace.onAnswer` is set, it runs that command with the document id as one more argument: the string is split into words as a shell does (quotes, backslash), a leading `~/` is the home folder, no shell runs, the working folder is the project root, it is stopped after 30 seconds and its output is dropped. The reply is `{"ok": true, "committed": <bool>, "handedOver": <bool>}`, where `handedOver` means the command is set and exited with 0. The notes folder `docs/inbox/notes` is watched too and only shown. `GET /diff` returns exactly what `docc diff <base> <head> --format json` prints (watch runs itself); both revisions are required, since `docc diff` has no working-tree side, and each must be a commit hash or a ref name by the rules of `git check-ref-format` (no leading `-`, no spaces, no `~^:?*[\`, `..` or `@{`, so `HEAD~1` is refused) before git sees it; requests come from 127.0.0.1 only; errors are `{"error": <text>}` with 400 for a bad or unknown revision and 500 otherwise.

`docc compile --format json` is for a program that shows the pages itself, such as Docspace. It prints one JSON object on one line and writes nothing: no `docs/out`, no source file. The object holds `$schema` (the version of its shape), `ok`, the `summary` and the full list of `diagnostics` as validate reports them, the `project` (title, lang, branding), the `tree` and the `pages` a reader sees, without hidden documents and notes. A page has its id, its path below src, title, kind, status, tags, parent, breadcrumbs, the one-line fields that open the page and the value fields, which form the property list (their text is not repeated in `blocks`; a property with an entry of `$decided` carries it as `decided`, like a block), each with its `label` (the `title` of the property in the kind schema, else the field name), whether it is a `folder` (it has children in the tree), its `icon` colour (its own or the nearest ancestor's, marked inherited), its `sections` (the headings of fields and `$sections`, with the anchor that links use as id) its `hash` (the version hash of the document), its `blocks`: JSON Pointer, the block `code` and version `hash`, source text, HTML (the same as in the HTML file) the section the block stands under and its entry of `$decided` as `decided`, and its `comments`: the readers' comments of `$comments` without their email, each with its place (same, changed or lost). The object is printed in every case: with errors of the groups 1xx or 2xx the tree and the pages are empty, and a failure (a bad `docc.json`, an unknown revision) is one diagnostic of code `config`, `usage` or `error` with exit code 2. The exit code is that of validate. `--hidden` also compiles the hidden documents: they join `pages` and `tree` in their place and carry `"hidden": true` (the field is absent on the others); their notes stay out, the diagnostics and `ok` are the same as without the flag (a visible document that links to a hidden one is still DOC210), and numbers and links are those of a full build. `--rev` compiles the tree of a Git revision (a commit, branch or tag) without a checkout: every file of the project comes from that revision, read with `git ls-tree` and `git cat-file --batch`, so includes and links resolve in it and the positions of the diagnostics are those of its files. In a bare repository `--config docs/docc.json` names the project folder. `docc schema compile` prints the JSON Schema of the object (`urn:docc:schema:compile:3`).

`docc workspace --format json` prints in one line everything a reader of the project shows (`urn:docc:schema:workspace:1`, `docc schema workspace`): `compile`, the object of `docc compile --hidden`; `roles`, the kinds that play the roles of tasks, checks, events, questions and meetings (the documents of a meetings kind are marked hidden in the tree of `compile`: the reader lists them in their own tab), copied from the `workspace` section of `docc.json` (a kind or a list of kinds); `coverage`, one row per block its kind schema wants covered by code (`x-docc-covered`), with its text, the code tags that name it sorted into the areas of the section (a tag no area matches is `code`), and `manual` from a `docIgnore` of DOC404 on it (its reason, and `by`: human or agent); `history`, the commits of `docc log`, newest first, at most 200, each with its `trailers` and `actor` (human or agent: the trailer `Crew-Actor`, else agent for a subject starting with `crew-` or `PRD:`); `notes`, every `*.md` file in `docs/inbox/notes/`, newest first, with its title (the first heading, else the file name), text and time; `run`, the content of the run file, or null; and `generatedAt`. docc knows nothing of the tool that writes the section. It writes nothing.

`docc log --format json` and `docc diff <base> <head> --format json` give the same program the history, read from Git without a checkout (a bare mirror with `--config` too). `docc log` lists the commits of the first-parent chain of `--rev` (default HEAD) that changed anything in the source folder, newest first, down to `--since` (not included; a commit off that chain is an error): full hashes, parents, author, committer, date, subject and body, and each changed file with its status (A, M, D, R with the old path), id, title, how many blocks it added, changed and removed and their codes (a changed block gives the code it has after the change, a removed one the code it had; a block with no code yet is only counted), so a program can tell which paragraphs changed. A deleted document keeps its last title, a file that is not valid JSON is marked broken and counted against its last good version, a document hidden in that version is marked hidden (with its counts; the version that shows it counts all its blocks as added, as the diff does), and a change only inside the top-level `$comments` is comments-only (a commit is when all its files are). `docc diff` compiles each side from its own revision, as `docc compile --rev` does, and lines up the blocks of every changed document: an operation same, add, rm or ch with the block on each side in the shape of compile; without `--path` only the changes, with `--path` one document with every block in an order for two columns. The base may be the empty tree, for a root commit. Both use the one alignment of blocks the HTML history uses, so the counts of the log are the operations of the diff. `docc schema log` and `docc schema diff` print their JSON Schemas.

`docc check` is read-only and made for CI. It runs validate (a block without a code is DOC216, a link whose version hash is missing or old is DOC209, a code fingerprint that does not match is DOC402), then compares `docs/out` with what the sources produce, with or without the comments and with or without the block codes of `--codes` (DOC501; not with `"commitOut": false`). With errors of the groups 1xx or 2xx the comparison is skipped. `docc check <paths>` takes files or folders, relative to the current folder or absolute, inside the project: it still loads and checks the whole project and builds the whole graph, but reports only the diagnostics of files under the paths, and the exit code and the warning limit count only those; `docs/out` is compared only when a path is `docs/out`, lies in it or above it. It is for the pre-commit hook of one part of a project, such as a git submodule whose hook runs `cd .. && docc check backend`: an unfinished edit in another part does not block its commit, and the full check stays with the hook of the whole project. With paths, DOC404 also reports a block whose tag stood under a path at HEAD of the Git repository that holds the path (a submodule's own, read with git, not from the disk) and that no tag names now: the change removes its last tag, so the diagnostic stands at the place of that tag and passes the path filter. A block nobody has tagged yet is not reported this way; the full check reports it. A path outside a Git work tree skips this part. `docc validate <paths>` scopes its report the same way.

`docc codes` gives a code to every block that has none (the key of its document and the next number) and writes `key` into a document that needs one; it cuts the code from a value field, which an older docc gave one, and says how many; and does nothing else: it never changes a code or a hash and checks nothing. A program that writes documents (Docspace) runs it so that the blocks it writes get their codes at once. `docc migrate` moves a project of an old format (codes of four signs; or a `docc.lock`, named anchors and links without hashes) once: a key for every document and a code of it for every block, links, includes, comments and the `id#^code` in code files rewritten, hashes and fingerprints that matched kept matching and the missing ones written, `docc.lock` deleted; a link the lock held unconfirmed gets a hash that does not match. Running it again changes nothing. Until then every other command refuses a project with a lock ("run docc migrate") and reports each old code as DOC216.

`docc ack <file>:<line>` confirms one place an agent has just read after DOC209 or DOC402: it writes the hash the target has now into the stale link of that line (two links to the same target on one line are one place), or into the stale target of a `docc:` tag, or the fingerprint the code has now into that tag, and prints what it wrote. When the line holds more than one thing to confirm, the target after the place picks one (`#^PAY-14`, `[[b#^PAY-14]]`, or `~` for the fingerprint); otherwise it refuses with exit code 2 and names them. It has no globs and no form for many places.

`docc update` replaces the running binary with a release from GitHub. It reads `checksums.txt` of the release, picks the archive for this system, refuses it when the SHA-256 differs and only then swaps the file. The flag check only reports whether a newer release exists (exit code 1: there is one), the flag version takes a given tag. A development build without a release version refuses to update. The variable DOCC_BASE_URL replaces the releases address, `install.sh` and `install.ps1` read it too.

`docc comments` handles the readers' comments, which live in the documents themselves, in the top-level member `$comments` ([Document model](document-model.md#comments)). Without a subcommand (or with list) it prints every comment with its document, the text of its block now and its place: same, changed (the block was edited) or lost (no block at its pointer, its words are gone, or the answered form field is not there). `docc comments apply` reads a JSON array of operations from standard input, add (a document id or path and the comment; a missing id and creation time are filled in), rm (an id) and edit (an id and the text that replaces the old one, or for an answer to a form field the answer, ratings or flag and note that replace it, what is left out going: the comment stays an answer to the same field, follows the field if it moved, quotes it as it reads now and keeps its creation time; every edit keeps `created` and sets `edited` to the time now, in UTC like `created`, a second edit overwrites it, and add never sets it), and edits the files in place: only `$comments` changes and every other byte of a file stays; a `$comments` that was not there is added as the last member of the document, indented like the file, and it goes away with its last comment. A comment stands only where a reader looks, one rule for the CLI, the import and Docspace: `at` must be the pointer of a block, a property or (for an answer) the form field that `docc compile` shows on the page of that document, so notes, `docIgnore`, `hidden`, the title and `$comments` itself are refused; `quote` is always the source text of that block, and a quote given is replaced. A hidden document takes no comment, and rm and edit leave its comments alone, unless `--hidden` is given (an agent working by hand; Docspace never gives it). rm and edit refuse an id that more than one comment of the project has (DOC112). While the project has errors of groups 1xx-2xx readers see no page, so add is refused. One bad operation fails the batch with exit code 2 and nothing is written; with `--format json` it prints what it added (with the ids it made), removed and edited and the files it wrote, in the shape `docc schema comments-apply` prints. `docc comments import <file>` (`-` reads the copied text from standard input) writes the comments of the HTML file, copied as text or downloaded, into their documents through apply: a comment already there (same id) is skipped, a comment left on an older build follows its block to where it stands now, an answer goes to its form field, and a comment that would not stand where a reader looks (a hidden document or part, a block that is gone) is skipped and listed, like one on a page that is gone. `docc comments rm <id>` deletes comments through apply; an id may be shortened to a unique prefix. There are no statuses and no replies: a comment that was handled is deleted in the same commit as the fix.

Every command accepts --help and prints its flags with an example. The global flags may stand before or after the command. `docc init` ends with a Next block of steps.

`docc explain` takes a code in any case (doc209), a name (style/hedging) or a group (graph, style): a rule with an example, or for a group the list of its rules. `docc rules` lists the rules with their effective levels; `docc schema document`, `docc schema config`, `docc schema compile`, `docc schema workspace`, `docc schema log` and `docc schema diff` print the JSON Schemas.

The settings are in [Configuration](config.md) and the generated pages in [Rendering](rendering.md).

## Flags

format text or json, config, max-diagnostics (default 20, errors first, applies to both formats, 0 means no limit, negative values are rejected), max-warnings.

## Exit codes

0: clean.

1: errors, or more effective warnings than the limit.

2: wrong usage or configuration, including a missing source folder or a kind schema that does not load. The message goes to stderr; with `--format json` it is the usual report (`summary`, `diagnostics`) with diagnostics of code `config`, `usage` or `error`, and every error of `docc.json` is listed at once.
